primitives.name: Ball as Game
primitives.verbatim_quote: For the ball, as it lay there, was the game.
primitives.assumptions: The ball represents the entire state of the game; all strategic decisions converge on its possession.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the ball loses its centrality, the game's information structure collapses into noise.

layer2.mapping: GSI: The ball's position maps to the posterior distribution over outcomes. GSE: The ball's trajectory encodes the optimal policy's next move.
layer2.telemetry: Ball possession percentage and turnover rates

primitives.name: Battle of Wits
primitives.verbatim_quote: Between these two men lay the real issue of the crisis.
primitives.assumptions: Two rational agents face a binary decision under incomplete information, each trying to outguess the other.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Pure randomness eliminates the strategic layer, reducing the interaction to a coin flip.

layer2.mapping: GSI: This is a zero-sum Bayesian game with imperfect information. GSE: The optimal strategy involves mixed policies to avoid predictability.
layer2.telemetry: Player positioning data and reaction time metrics

primitives.name: Temptation to Think of Self
primitives.verbatim_quote: If ever a football player faced the temptation to think of himself and his own advantage it was that man in that moment.
primitives.assumptions: An agent prioritizes immediate local gain over global team objective, creating a conflict between selfish and cooperative incentives.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Selfish behavior leads to a non-cooperative Nash equilibrium that sub-optimizes overall system performance.

layer2.mapping: GSI: This is a principal-agent problem where individual utility diverges from team value. GSE: Local reward maximization can destabilize long-term state transitions.
layer2.telemetry: Individual player performance vs. team outcome correlation

primitives.name: Three of Them Almost Equally Close
primitives.verbatim_quote: There were three of them almost equally close to it, one the back who had failed to catch it and the others the two defending players who had swept out with the end.
primitives.assumptions: Three equidistant agents simultaneously compete for a single resource, introducing geometric uncertainty into the decision tree.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Degeneracy occurs when distances become indistinguishable within measurement error, eliminating clear priority.

layer2.mapping: GSI: This creates a symmetric information set where no agent has a first-mover advantage. GSE: State transitions become stochastic due to overlapping action zones.
layer2.telemetry: Spatial proximity metrics and collision probability calculations

The core mathematical structure is a sequential decision process under uncertainty. The 'Battle of Wits' (primitive 2) models this as a zero-sum game where two defenders must coordinate to block the ball carrier while avoiding predictable patterns. The 'Temptation to Think of Self' (primitive 3) introduces a principal-agent tension—individual utility versus team value. When an agent exploits local advantage, they create exploitable regularity, undermining the defender's ability to maintain a robust blocking zone. The 'Three of Them Almost Equally Close' (primitive 4) adds geometric complexity: if distances are indistinguishable within sensor noise, the decision becomes probabilistic rather than deterministic. The 'Ball as Game' (primitive 1) anchors the entire system—possession is the sufficient statistic for victory. Mathematically, this maps to a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the ball's location defines the state, actions are player movements, and rewards are scoring opportunities. The epistemic challenge is to infer the opponent's private belief distribution over the ball's trajectory given noisy observations of their body language and prior behavior.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Each defender must model the ball-carrier's intention as a rational agent seeking maximum utility (touchdown). Conversely, the ball-carrier models the defenders' coordination as a cooperative threat. Mutual best-response requires each player to randomize their decision to prevent the others from exploiting their predictability. The equilibrium concept is a correlated mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium.
